title: Watch the sunrise

segments.voice: Yesterday, moral beauty, and the warm lift of seeing goodness. Your line was elevation. Whose kindness did you pass on? The scientists have had their turn. Now we move to practices of awe, starting with a show that opens every morning. Day one thousand thirty-four.

Before the alarm, the window is the color of dishwater. Nothing has happened yet. Then the edge of the sky goes pale, then pink, then a color with no good name. Birds start before there's anything to see. The rooftops come out of the dark one by one. And then, at a single point on the horizon, a sliver of fire. Nobody pressed a button. Nobody earned it. It just arrives, the way it arrived yesterday and the day before, mostly while we were asleep.
screen: `THE COLOR OF DISHWATER.` → `PALE, PINK, NO GOOD NAME.` → `A SLIVER OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Today the practice is the lesson: watch one sunrise, all the way through. First, why it works on people. A sunrise is vast and it is slow. You can't hurry it and you can't pause it. For once, the day comes to you, instead of you chasing the day. Second, in several traditions, the hours around dawn hold a special place in prayer. Muslims pray the dawn prayer, Fajr, before the sun comes up. Jews say the morning prayers of Shacharit as the day begins. Some Hindus offer water to the rising sun. Each tradition has its own reasons, and they aren't the same reasons. But each one gathers near the hours when the light changes. Third, a poet's picture. In the book of Psalms, the sun comes out "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race." A wedding and a race, at once. The psalm makes the sun sound eager, as if it's been waiting all night to begin. Fourth, Thoreau's warning. Near the very end of Walden he writes a line about dawn that isn't about the sky at all: "Only that day dawns to which we are awake." The sun comes up whether anyone is watching. But a day you sleep through, in body or in attention, never quite dawns for you. Watching a sunrise is a way of being awake for one, on purpose, start to finish. It arrives. The only question is whether anyone is there to meet it.
screen: `VAST, SLOW, AND UNEARNED.` · `PRAYERS AT THE CHANGING LIGHT.` · `A BRIDEGROOM, A RUNNER.` · `ONLY THAT DAY DAWNS TO WHICH WE ARE AWAKE.` · then, large: `IT ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Turn toward the brightest window you have, or the brightest part of the room. If it's early and the sky is changing, watch it. If not, close your eyes and bring back a sunrise you've seen, or one you can imagine from where you sit. Follow it slowly: the dark, the pale edge, the colors, the first sliver. Don't rush to the end. Let the light come to you. Breathe as if you have all the time it takes. The bell holds the time.
Fajr. The Muslim dawn prayer, said before the sun comes up, one of several traditions' ways of greeting the whole arrival of a day. Today's word.
Your line: it arrives. Check when the sun comes up where you live, and set one alarm this week to watch it, start to finish, with no phone in your hand. Day one thousand thirty-four.

howItsDone: People who make a practice of watching the sunrise get up before dawn, go somewhere with a view of the eastern sky, and watch quietly from first light until the sun is up; in several traditions, morning prayers gather around the hours of dawn.

notes: Editor: the Thoreau line is in Walden's closing paragraph but is not its last sentence; 'He ends Walden with' changed to 'Near the very end of Walden'.

Descriptions of dawn practice in three traditions (Fajr before sunrise; Shacharit as the morning prayer; some Hindus offering water to the rising sun) are brief and unranked; confirm each is fair and that 'in several traditions, the hours around dawn hold a special place in prayer' is acceptable phrasing.
Auditor: smoothed the garbled line 'none of them is the same as the others' and softened 'at the moment the light changes' (Shacharit may be said through the morning, not only at first light).
Psalm 19:5 and Walden's closing line quoted from memory; confirm wording.
The psalm reading ('makes the sun sound eager') is the script's own gloss; confirm it is fair.
